attributes.morphology: fibers extended over the direction of deformation

evidence.quote: In the as-delivered state the macrostructure of molybdenum alloys is represented by fibers extended over the direction of the deformation.
The dislocation structure of the alloy is cellular. The size of the cells is about 2 μm, and the dislocation density is not high.
Specifically, the process of primary recrystallization in alloy TsM-10 ends after a 1-h annealing at 1150°C and polyhedral grains 10 μm in size are formed.

After a 1-h annealing at 1300°C the macrostructure of high-temperature molybdenum alloys TsM-6 and TsM-12 alloyed with zirconium and hafnium virtually does not change, but the polygonization results in the appearance of subgrains 4 - 6 μm in size.
Annealing at 1500°C for 1 h is accompanied by recrystallization of the metal and a grain growth to 40 - 50 μm.
Annealing for 1 h at 1700 and 1850°C increases the grain size to 200 and 300 μm due to the processes of collective and secondary recrystallization.

A typical feature of sheet molybdenum alloys annealed at 1100 - 1500°C is the fact that the recrystallization fully ends only in the bulk of the metal, whereas surface layers up to 0.1 mm thick remain nonrecrystallized.

attributes.morphology: even, plane, and extended boundaries parallel to the axis of the weld

evidence.quote: The structure of welds of molybdenum alloys is characterized by a quite large size of the crystallites (200 - 500 μm), the presence of even, plane, and extended boundaries parallel to the axis of the weld, and the formation of segregations of interstitial impurities on the boundaries due to the enrichment of the solid solution under the conditions of non-equilibrium crystallization and rapid cooling of the weld [2].

The high-temperature embrittlement of molybdenum is commonly connected with the segregation of Mo2C-type carbides over grain boundaries (these carbides are thermodynamically stable at 1700 - 2100°C) and with the change in the fracture behavior from ductile transcrystallite to intercrystallite [3, 14].

evidence.quote: Alloys TsM-6 and TsM-12 contain up to 0.2 wt.% zirconium and hafnium and belong to high-temperature molybdenum alloys with solid-solution hardening.

The high-temperature embrittlement of molybdenum is commonly connected with the segregation of Mo2C-type carbides over grain boundaries (these carbides are thermodynamically stable at 1700 - 2100°C) and with the change in the fracture behavior from ductile transcrystallite to intercrystallite [3, 14].

The growth in high-temperature short-term strength of deformed molybdenum alloys after annealing at 1150-1850°C seems to be connected with the special feature of the structural transformations that occur in active static stretching of the specimen under dynamic conditions. It is known that high-temperature annealing under stress causes more rapid rest and recrystallization of the deformed metal than annealing without stress, which is explained by the accelerated migration of grain boundaries and subboundaries.
